message:
A storm moves into Colorado on Thursday night, favoring northwest Colorado and the Flat Tops. Upper elevations of the Flat Tops may pick up around 10 inches of snow accompanied by strong southwest winds. Where snow falls on bare ground at lower elevations, there will be no avalanche concerns or increase in danger. However, higher elevations with a layer of old snow on northerly slopes may see a few small avalanches.

With so much bare ground still exposed, hikers and hunters may continue traveling to the high peaks of the Flat Tops Wilderness. If you are heading into this area, use caution when crossing steep, snow-covered slopes facing northwest, north, or northeast.

Snowfall forecasts vary considerably among weather models for the Park Range, adding uncertainty to the outlook. We are leaning toward the lower snowfall forecast, which is why we are not increasing danger at upper elevations of the Mt. Zirkel Wilderness. If you are traveling in the Zirkels, use caution if snowfall exceeds expectations. The high peaks, generally above 11,000 feet, may have a layer of old snow on northerly slopes that could serve as a weak foundation for new wind-drifted snow.

Elsewhere, snowfall forecasts are much lower, and less old snow remains on the ground. There is just enough snow cover in places like Summit County, the EJMT, and near Cameron Pass for weak layers to develop. Farther east, however, snow coverage is too sparse to support a continuous weak layer. In areas without old, faceted snow, avalanche danger is unlikely to increase until more consistent snowfall builds a slab over the existing weak snow.

Images.caption: Looking west from the top of Loveland Pass on November 15. You can see there isn't quite enough snow to overcome surface roughness on these north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, but maybe enough to form a weak layer in the future.
Images.altText: A rounded alpine ridge with patchy snow cover

Images.caption: The north-facing slopes of Red Peak from Hoosier Pass on November 12. This is one of the snowier areas in the Northern Mountains right now.
This image from the Sentinel Weekly satellite on Caltopo shows the patchy snow cover age in the Northern Mountains. These areas of white are thin and patchy, but also weak and faceted.
Images.altText: A satellite image showing thin strips of snow in the Northern Mountains and a whole lot of greenery.

message:
A well-documented weak layer lurks in our upper snowpack, between a few inches and up to a foot deep below the snow surface. An uptick in small avalanches in the snowiest parts of the Central Mountains point to how little new snow the weak layer can hold. We know the weak layer is distributed on many west through north to east-facing slopes near and above treeline, across the Central Mountains.

An incoming storm will bring a trace to a couple of inches across most of the Central Mountains throughout the day Friday, with favored areas in the Elk Mountains possibly getting around 3 to 6 inches. In this snowier area, that may be all the snow we need to develop a more cohesive slab across much of the terrain that has buried weak layers. With this much snow expected before the end of the day Friday, we are transitioning to a Persistent Slab avalanche problem as we expect remotely triggered avalanches to come into play and expect this problem to linger for some time as continued snow builds this slab on top of persistent weak layers. Any slabs will likely not be broadly connected across multiple terrain features, and most avalanches are expected to be small, but in wind-drifted areas you may be able to trigger a D2, so carefully assess slab development as you travel on the north half of the compass.

Images.caption: A small amount of recent snow has buried and preserved a delicate weak layer. The thin layer just below the new snow is buried surface hoar, which can be particularly nasty once a thicker slab builds on top.
Images.altText: A black glove next to a small snow pit

Images.caption: This fresh Storm Slab avalanche is a good indication of what's in store when we get more snow and wind. Many slopes on the north half of the compass have a buried weak layer, just waiting for a more connected slab to set things off.
Images.altText: A fresh slab avalanche below a rocky face

Images.caption: Watch for small avalanches like these in steep, shady terrain, especially as we get more snow. They may not bury you, but they can knock you down into rockier terrain below.
Images.altText: Small loose snow avalanches below a ridge

message:
This week's snow and wind created drifts that sit on top of a weak, faceted snowpack. With more snow and wind on the way the snowpack remains reactive. Field reports continue to come in of remotely triggered avalanches near and above treeline. As a result we transitioned from a Wind Slab avalanche problem to a Persistent Slab avalanche problem.

The current weather models indicate that this weekend's storm will not be a big producer for the Southern Mountains. Continue to pay close attention to changing conditions as you travel. Suspect drifts may not exist on every slope, but if you find the wrong slope you could trigger an avalanche.

Images.caption: The snowpack is deep for this time of the year in the San Juan Mountains. This photo from the Wilson Group outside of Telluride shows just how caked the mountains look. These folks also found more than 2 meters of snow on the ground on a northwest-facing slope above treeline. Snow cover becomes patchy at lower elevations and on the eastern edge of the Southern Mountains.

The last snowfall event was on November 2nd, and since then, high pressure weather has weakened the snow surface. We now have widespread near-surface facets and surface hoar on top of the snowpack, which became our first buried weak layer of the season.
